name: Crab Ride
description: Crab ride controls hips from below or behind with hooks behind the knees to create back exposure. The crab ride is a dynamic back-control entry used when the opponent is standing, kneeling, or in turtle.
shortInstruction: From behind or below, hook both feet behind the opponent's knees, squeeze your heels toward their glutes, and pull their hips toward your chest. Walk your hands up their back to expose the back.
summary: The crab ride uses hooks behind the opponent's knees to control their hips from a distance, then walks hand-over-hand up their back to collapse their posture and expose the back. It is most commonly used from the truck position, from turtle, or from back control when the opponent stands up. The system relies on the principle that controlling the hips from behind with knee hooks gives you leverage to fold the opponent forward.
whyItWorks: Knee hooks (feet behind their knees) give you control of their lower body from a safe distance — they cannot kick or base out
Pulling their hips toward your chest while squeezing the knee hooks folds their body forward, collapsing their posture
Walking hands up their back (hand-over-hand) progressively breaks their posture until they are folded over
The crab ride works from standing, kneeling, or turtle — it is a universal back-entry system
commonMistakes: Letting the hips separate from your chest — the crab ride requires hip-to-chest connection to control posture
Losing the knee hooks — once the hooks are lost, the opponent can stand up or turn into you
Walking hands too fast up the back — each hand placement must be secure before advancing
Not keeping heels squeezed toward the glutes — loose hooks can be pummeled out
coachingCues: Walk the hands, one at a time
Fold them forward to expose the back
safetySummary: Knee hooks should be placed behind the knees, not in the back of the knee joint — direct pressure on the knee joint can cause hyperextension
Do not pull backward aggressively with the knee hooks — this can strain the opponent's hamstrings or knee ligaments
When walking hands up the back, be careful not to place pressure on the spine
keyCorrections: If the opponent stands up and breaks the hooks: re-hook immediately by stepping inside their stance and placing the hooks again
If they are too strong to fold: alternate between pulling hips and pushing their head with your hands
If you lose one hook: keep the other hook and re-establish the second before advancing

systemLogic.corePrinciple: The crab ride has three phases: Establish Hooks: Collapse Posture → Secure Back

decisionTree.action: from behind the opponent (standing, kneeling, or turtle), place both feet inside their legs and hook behind both knees. Squeeze your heels toward their glutes

pull their hips toward your chest with the knee hooks while walking your hands hand-over-hand up their spine. Each hand placement should advance toward the back of their neck. As your hands climb, their posture collapses forward
once they are folded forward, release one hook and replace it with a traditional body triangle or seatbelt grip. Slide your knee into their hip line and secure full back control
release one hook, place your foot on their glute, and push them forward. This creates the forward fold you need

moneyDetails: The crab ride is the most effective way to take the back from the truck or turtle — it is a high-value transition in both wrestling and BJJ
Mastering the crab ride gives you a reliable back entry from positions where traditional back takes fail
The crab ride is particularly effective against larger opponents because it uses leverage (knee hooks) rather than upper body strength
fixItFast: If they stand up and run away: release the hooks, chase, and re-hook from standing
If they turn into you: release the hooks and switch to a front headlock or body lock
If they sit back into you: keep the hooks, squeeze, and pull them onto their back
